questions.q: What does it mean for a sorting algorithm to be stable?
options: It runs in guaranteed O(n log n) worst-case time.
It preserves the relative order of records with equal keys.
It operates without allocating any additional memory on heap.
questions.fact: A sorting algorithm is stable if it preserves the relative order of records with equal keys.
why: O(n log n) complexity is an efficiency metric, not stability.
Stability guarantees that identical keys retain their initial relative order.
Sorting without additional memory defines in-place sorting, not stability.

questions.q: What defines an in-place sorting algorithm?
options: It sorts an array in linear O(n) time.
It never swaps elements during its execution passes.
It uses O(1) auxiliary memory beyond the input array.
questions.fact: An in-place sorting algorithm uses O(1) auxiliary memory beyond the input array.
why: In-place refers to auxiliary memory usage, not time complexity.
Many in-place sorts like quicksort and bubble sort perform swaps.
In-place algorithms require at most constant extra memory to rearrange items.

questions.q: How does bubble sort order elements, and what is its worst-case complexity?
options: It repeatedly compares and swaps adjacent out-of-order elements in O(n²).
It divides arrays recursively into halves in O(n log n).
It selects the global minimum element in O(n) time.
questions.fact: Bubble sort repeatedly compares and swaps adjacent out-of-order elements and runs in O(n²) worst-case time.
why: Bubble sort passes through neighbours, taking quadratic time when reversed.
Dividing arrays into halves describes merge sort, not bubble sort.
Selecting the minimum element is selection sort, which takes O(n²).

questions.q: What is the worst-case time complexity of merge sort?
options: O(n²) time when the array is sorted backwards.
O(n log n) time across all input orderings.
O(n) time when the array is already sorted.
questions.fact: Merge sort divides the array in half, recursively sorts both halves, and merges them in O(n log n) time.
why: Merge sort never degrades to O(n²); divisions remain balanced.
Halving log n times and merging in linear time ensures O(n log n).
Merge sort always performs full splits and merges, taking O(n log n).

questions.q: What strategy allows quicksort to achieve O(n log n) average time complexity?
options: It builds a sorted prefix by shifting items right.
It compares every pair of elements using parallel threads.
It partitions elements around a pivot value.
questions.fact: Quicksort partitions elements around a pivot value and achieves O(n log n) average time.
why: Shifting items into a prefix is insertion sort, not quicksort.
Quicksort does not compare all pairs or use parallel threads.
Partitioning puts smaller items left and larger items right of pivot.

questions.q: When does quicksort degrade to its worst-case time complexity of O(n²)?
options: When an unbalanced pivot is chosen repeatedly during partitioning.
When the array size is not an exact power of two.
When keys are compared using floating point arithmetic operations.
questions.fact: Quicksort can degrade to O(n²) worst-case time when an unbalanced pivot is chosen repeatedly.
why: Unbalanced pivots reduce problem size by only one, producing O(n²) work.
Array sizes that are not powers of two do not degrade quicksort.
Floating point comparison cost is constant O(1) and does not degrade complexity.

questions.q: What is the theoretical lower bound for comparison-based sorting in the worst case?
options: Ω(n) comparisons for any input array.
Ω(n²) comparisons across all comparison algorithms.
Ω(n log n) comparisons in the worst case.
questions.fact: Any comparison-based sorting algorithm requires Ω(n log n) comparisons in the worst case.
why: Linear comparisons are insufficient to distinguish all n! permutations.
O(n log n) algorithms like merge sort disprove an Ω(n²) lower bound.
A decision tree of n! outcomes requires a minimum height of Ω(n log n).
